candidate.stem: Two safety research groups agree on everything except timing: the first expects AI able to automate ML research within about a decade, the second in about fifty years. Which difference between their research plans follows from that one disagreement?

options.text: The first should favour methods that work on current systems and scale fast; the second can invest in foundational theory
The first should favour foundational theory that settles the problem at once; the second can refine methods for current systems
options.provenance: reverses the pairing in the 2030-vs-2050 paragraph, where 'breathing room for fundamental alignment research' belongs to the long case

options.text: Both should pursue the same portfolio of projects, with the first simply running it on a much tighter schedule
options.provenance: misreads 'we need safety solutions working soon' as a change of pace only, missing 'There's no time for slow theoretical research—we need approaches that work with current systems'

options.text: The second should defer most of its safety work until systems closer to transformative AI exist to study directly
options.provenance: the wait-and-see prior that forecasting has no bearing on what to do now, against the bold lead 'Predicting when AI automates cognitive labor determines which safety strategies are viable' and the long case's list of work to do in the breathing room

candidate.explanation: Timeline length changes which strategies are viable, not only how fast to carry them out. If AI can automate ML research within a decade, slow theoretical programmes may not finish in time, so the work has to function on current systems and scale quickly. Fifty years buys room for fundamental alignment research, robust governance and evaluation methods we can trust. The 'same portfolio, tighter schedule' option is the most tempting misreading. It treats a timeline as a deadline on a fixed plan, when a short timeline takes some projects off the table altogether. The reversed option swaps the pairing, because foundational theory is what the long case can afford. And a long timeline is room to do that deep work now, not a reason to wait. (Forecasting Timelines)
candidate.takeaway: A shorter timeline doesn't just speed up the safety agenda; it changes which items can be on it.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who took in the opening paragraph produces 'short: work with current systems; long: room for fundamental research' unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick 'same portfolio, faster', which is the intuitive default, or be torn between the key and its mirror image; 'current systems' and 'foundational theory' each appear in two options, so no word match marks the key, and the decade/fifty-year figures are hypotheticals in the stem rather than forecast dates.
